questions.question: How do you add and correctly remove a DOM event listener?
questions.title: Adding and removing listeners
questions.direct_answer: Use addEventListener with an event type and callback, then pass the same type, the same callback object, and the same capture setting to removeEventListener. Recreating an identical-looking arrow function does not remove the original listener because it has a different function identity.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether listener identity and lifetime are understood.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to remove a newly created anonymous function.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Using AbortSignal for grouped, explicit cleanup.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: addEventListener keeps a reference to the callback object.
removeEventListener needs the same type, callback identity, and capture value.
Store a named function when manual removal is needed.
An AbortSignal can remove a group of listeners together.
Avoid duplicate lifecycle registration that outlives its component.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`addEventListener` registers a callback on an event target without replacing other listeners for the same event. The registration is identified by the event type, callback identity, and capture setting.

For example, if code adds `() => save()` and later removes another `() => save()`, nothing is removed because each arrow expression creates a new function object. Storing the callback in `handleSave` lets both calls use the same identity.

The options object can control capture, one-time execution, passive behaviour, and an abort signal. For lifecycle cleanup, an `AbortController` is convenient because several listeners can share its signal and `abort()` removes them together.

Removal matters when a long-lived node or global object holds a callback that closes over component state. The listener can keep that state reachable and can run again after the component is gone. A listener on a node that becomes unreachable with its callback is normally collectible, so the real boundary is retained references and unwanted behaviour, not a rule that every listener always leaks.

sections.title: Listener removal is an identity operation
sections.content: The browser cannot infer that two functions have the same source text or intention. It records the exact callback object supplied at registration.

sections.title: Capture participates in matching
sections.content:
Most options do not need to match during removal, but the capture flag does. A capture listener and bubble listener using the same callback are distinct registrations. A stored options object is not required; the matching capture boolean is what matters.

Adding the same callback with the same type and capture does not create another identical registration, even if other option values differ. This detail should not replace clear lifecycle ownership.

questions.question: What do the once, passive, and signal event-listener options do?
questions.title: Event listener options
questions.direct_answer: once removes a listener after its first invocation, passive promises that the listener will not call preventDefault, and signal removes the listener when its AbortSignal is aborted. These options express lifecycle and cancellation behaviour directly, but each must match the event's real needs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether listener options are connected to exact lifecycle semantics.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separating phase selection from cleanup options.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: once automatically unregisters after the first invocation.
passive promises not to cancel the event's default action.
signal unregisters when its AbortController aborts.
capture chooses the capture phase and is separate from these lifecycle options.
Do not mark a listener passive if it must prevent a default action.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Listener options make behaviour explicit at registration. `{ once: true }` is for a callback that should run at most once; the browser removes it after it is invoked.

`{ passive: true }` promises that the callback will not call `preventDefault`. For example, a passive touch or wheel observer lets the browser begin scrolling without waiting for JavaScript to decide whether scrolling will be cancelled.

`{ signal }` ties listener lifetime to an `AbortController`. Aborting the controller removes the listener, and one signal can own several related listeners. This is useful for a widget that registers pointer, keyboard, and window listeners and needs one cleanup operation.

These options are not interchangeable. `once` is based on first invocation, while `signal` follows an external lifecycle. `passive` is a performance and behaviour promise, not a request to run in the background. I choose only the options supported by the event contract and keep `capture` explicit when the listener needs the capture phase.

sections.title: Options describe when and how a listener participates
sections.content: The callback still receives an ordinary Event object. Options change its phase, cancellation promise, and lifetime rather than its business logic.

sections.title: Automatic cleanup removes timing ambiguity
sections.content:
Manual removal in several exit paths is easy to miss. A shared abort signal creates one ownership boundary, while `once` handles a single-use action even if the first event arrives earlier than expected.

A passive listener that calls `preventDefault` cannot cancel the event. It should not be used for custom drag or gesture code that genuinely suppresses native scrolling; that interaction also needs suitable CSS such as `touch-action`.

sections.title: Listener option contracts
sections.content:
| Option | Promise or trigger | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `once` | Remove after first invocation | One-time initialization |
| `passive` | Never cancel default action | Scroll observation |
| `signal` | Remove when aborted | Component cleanup |
| `capture` | Run on capture phase | Early path observation |

questions.question: How do CustomEvent and dispatchEvent work?
questions.title: Custom DOM events
questions.direct_answer: CustomEvent creates an application-defined DOM event and can carry data in its detail property. dispatchEvent sends it synchronously through the target's event system. Bubbling, cancellation, and shadow-boundary crossing are false unless requested, so the event's public contract should set those options deliberately.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether custom events have a precise propagation and timing contract.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming custom events bubble automatically or dispatch asynchronously.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Choosing events for decoupled notification rather than every function call.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: CustomEvent carries application data in detail.
dispatchEvent invokes listeners synchronously before returning.
Custom events do not bubble unless bubbles is true.
cancelable enables preventDefault and affects dispatchEvent's return value.
Use events to announce facts, not to expose mutable internal objects casually.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`CustomEvent` lets a DOM component announce an application-specific fact through the same listener system as built-in events. The event name describes what happened, and the optional `detail` field carries related data.

For example, a product picker can dispatch `product-selected` with `{ id: 42 }` after its internal selection changes. A parent can listen without calling a private method or knowing the picker's internal markup.

`dispatchEvent` is synchronous: matching listeners run before the call returns. The return value is false only when the event is cancelable and a listener successfully called `preventDefault`. Custom events do not bubble or cross a shadow root by default; `{ bubbles: true, composed: true }` must be an intentional component API choice.

The boundary is coupling. Events are good for one-to-many notification and component boundaries, but a direct function call is simpler when one known caller needs a result. Detail data should be stable and minimal because listeners receive the same object reference, not a protected copy.

sections.title: An event announces that something happened
sections.content: A useful event name is a past-tense fact or clear domain occurrence. The dispatcher should not need to know which listeners exist, and listeners should not have to inspect private DOM structure.

sections.title: Cancellation can form a veto contract
sections.content:
If a custom event is created with `cancelable: true`, a listener can call `preventDefault` to reject a proposed operation. The dispatcher checks the boolean returned by `dispatchEvent`. That pattern should be documented because it changes an announcement into a request that may be vetoed.

Exceptions thrown by event listeners do not propagate back as a normal exception from `dispatchEvent`; they are reported as uncaught exceptions. Dispatch is synchronous, but it is not a replacement for a promise-based request/response API.
